subChunks.title: Writing Genealogical Research Reports

storyBeats.txt: The report is the product, Theodora said. Everything else — the archive visits, the DNA analysis, the evidence evaluation — is process. The client receives the report. The court sees the report. The professional standard is measured by the report.

A research report that is technically brilliant but incomprehensible to the client has failed. A report that is beautifully written but poorly cited has failed. A report that omits negative results has failed. The standard is high because the purpose is serious.

Good genealogical report writing is a discipline in itself. It requires you to think clearly about what you know, what you don't know, and how you know what you know — and then communicate all three to someone who wasn't there.

subChunks.hookHtml:
A genealogical research report is the primary deliverable of professional genealogical practice. It communicates the findings of a research project to a client, to a court, to a probate solicitor, to an academic journal, or to posterity. It must be simultaneously technically rigorous (meeting GPS standards), practically useful (answering the client's question), and communicatively effective (readable by a non-specialist).

The ability to write clear, well-structured, fully cited reports is what separates a professional genealogist from a skilled hobbyist. It is also the skill most commonly tested in professional credentialling processes — BCG portfolio submissions and AGRA membership applications both require demonstrated report-writing competence.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Types of Genealogical Report

Genealogical reports take several forms depending on their purpose and audience:

  • Client research report: A narrative account of research conducted, findings, conclusions, and recommendations for further work. Written for a non-specialist audience. The most common type in professional practice.
  • Heir-location report: A formal document for solicitors and courts identifying proven heirs to an estate. Held to legal evidentiary standards; may be examined by opposing counsel. Must be unambiguously clear about what is proven and what is not.
  • Proof argument (NGSQ-style): An analytical essay for peer-reviewed publication or submission as expert testimony. Written for a specialist audience; fully footnoted; follows the GPS analytical framework.
  • Research summary/log report: A brief account of research conducted, sources searched, and results found — used for interim reporting and as a personal research log.

Structure of a Client Research Report

A professional client research report follows a standard structure:

  1. Header: Client name, report date, researcher's name and credentials, project reference number.
  2. Research objective: The specific question or task this report addresses, as agreed in the research plan.
  3. Summary of findings: A brief, accessible statement of the key findings — written first so the client can understand the conclusion before reading the detail.
  4. Methodology: What records were searched, in what order, and why. Includes negative results (records searched but yielding no relevant information). This section demonstrates the reasonably exhaustive search required by GPS.
  5. Findings in detail: A narrative account of what each record source contained, with the evidence analysed using the source/information/evidence framework. Citations in full for every source.
  6. Analysis and conclusions: How the evidence fits together; any conflicts and how they were resolved; the confidence level of each conclusion.
  7. Recommendations: What further research is possible or advisable; what records were not searched and why; what would resolve any remaining questions.
  8. Appendices: Copies of key documents (certified or digital); pedigree charts; DNA charts; correspondence with archives.

Tone and Register

Client reports should be written in plain English accessible to a non-specialist. Avoid technical jargon without explanation. Write in the third person for formal reports. Use precise language: 'the evidence indicates' rather than 'it appears' or 'I think'. State the epistemic status of every conclusion: 'This conclusion is based on three independent sources and is supported with reasonable confidence' is more helpful than 'probably correct'.

Avoid emotional language, even in sensitive cases (NPEs, adoption, unexpected findings). State findings matter-of-factly, then address the implications in a separate section if needed.

Citing Sources in Reports

Every factual assertion in a report must be accompanied by a footnote or endnote citing the specific source. Use Evidence Explained citation templates. If the report is for a non-specialist audience, consider using endnotes rather than footnotes so they do not interrupt the narrative. In heir-location reports and proof arguments written for legal or academic use, footnotes are standard.

Vague citations are not acceptable. 'Census records' is not a citation. 'England & Wales Census 1881, Wolverhampton, St Peter's sub-district, household of William Cooper; RG11/2881/45/3; digital image, Ancestry, accessed 12 March 2025' is a citation.

Negative Results

One of the most important — and most often omitted — components of a research report is the documentation of negative results: searches that were conducted but found nothing. A methodologically complete report tells the reader not only what was found but what was not found, so that a subsequent researcher does not duplicate the work and so that the reasoning for a negative conclusion can be evaluated.

'No marriage record for Elizabeth Cooper was found in the GRO index for England and Wales for the period 1850–1880, despite searches under multiple surname spellings' is meaningful genealogical information. Its omission from a report leaves a gap that could lead a future researcher to assume the search had never been done.

Reports for Sensitive Findings

Reports that disclose unexpected findings — non-paternity events, adoptions, previously unknown relatives — require particular care. The professional approach: state the findings factually; clearly distinguish what the DNA or documentary evidence shows from what it implies; and include a brief section offering the client guidance on further support (specialist organisations, counsellors). The report is a document; the conversation with the client is a separate matter and should occur before the report is delivered if the findings are likely to be distressing.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a 16-year-old why a professional genealogist needs to include not just what they found but also what they didn't find when writing a report for a client.
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml: Draft the 'Methodology' and 'Findings in detail' sections of a research report for the following scenario: You have been researching the parentage of William Hayes, baptised at Liverpool, Lancashire in 1852. You have found: (1) his baptism entry at St Nicholas's, Liverpool (father listed as John Hayes, mother Mary née Kelly); (2) his parents' marriage at St Nicholas's in 1849; (3) John Hayes in the 1841 census as a labourer in Liverpool; (4) no baptism for John Hayes found in Liverpool or adjacent parishes 1810–1825 despite a thorough search. Write these two sections in report style, correctly citing the hypothetical sources.
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
Methodology

The following records were searched in the course of this research:

The baptism register of St Nicholas's Church, Liverpool (Lancashire), for the period 1845–1855 was examined for William Hayes. The marriage registers of St Nicholas's, Liverpool for 1840–1855 were searched for a union between a Hayes and a Kelly. The 1841 England and Wales census was searched for John Hayes in Liverpool sub-registration districts. The baptism registers for the following Liverpool parishes were searched for a baptism of John Hayes between 1810 and 1825: St Nicholas's, St George's, St Peter's, St Luke's, St John's, and St Philip's. The Lancashire county baptism transcripts available via FindMyPast were searched phonetically for 'Hayes' and variant spellings ('Hays', 'Haies') for the same period. No baptism for a John Hayes was found in any of these searches within the specified parameters.

Findings in detail

The baptism register of St Nicholas's Church, Liverpool records the baptism of William Hayes on 14 March 1852, son of John Hayes, labourer, and Mary née Kelly.1 This is an original source providing primary information for William's parentage and approximate birth date.

A marriage entry in the same register records the marriage of John Hayes and Mary Kelly on 6 November 1849.2 Both parties signed with marks. This entry directly corroborates the baptism record's identification of William's parents.

The 1841 England and Wales census records a John Hayes, age 25 (b. c.1816), labourer, lodging in Scotland Road, Liverpool.3 This is consistent in name and occupation with the father named in the 1849 and 1852 church records. The age implies a birth year of approximately 1813–1818.

No baptism for John Hayes was found in the Liverpool parish registers searched (see Methodology). This negative evidence indicates that John Hayes was not baptised in Liverpool and may have been born elsewhere in Lancashire or Ireland. His Irish origin is plausible given his wife's Irish surname (Kelly) and his residence in Scotland Road, Liverpool — a neighbourhood heavily populated by Irish immigrants in this period. Further research in Irish records (Catholic diocesan registers, civil registration from 1864) would be required to establish his origin.

Citations:
1 St Nicholas's Church, Liverpool, baptism register, 14 March 1852, entry for William Hayes; Lancashire Parish Register Society transcript; digital image, FindMyPast, accessed 1 April 2025.
2 St Nicholas's Church, Liverpool, marriage register, 6 November 1849, entry for Hayes–Kelly; Lancashire Parish Register Society transcript; digital image, FindMyPast, accessed 1 April 2025.
3 England & Wales Census 1841, Scotland Road, Liverpool; HO107/581/12/15; digital image, Ancestry, accessed 1 April 2025.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: A client has received a research report from another genealogist that claims her great-great-grandmother, Bridget Murphy, was 'definitely born in County Cork, Ireland around 1845.' The report cites only a single source: 'Irish birth records, FamilySearch.' No specific record is cited, no other sources are mentioned, and no explanation is given for the 'around 1845' date. Evaluate this report against professional standards and explain what a professionally adequate report for this conclusion would need to contain.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
This report fails basic professional standards in several respects:

(1) Source citation: 'Irish birth records, FamilySearch' is not an acceptable citation. Civil registration in Ireland began in 1864; if Bridget was born c.1845, there would be no civil registration of her birth. The source is therefore likely a church record — but which church, which parish, which register, what the reference number is, and when it was accessed are all missing. A reader cannot locate this record. (2) Date claim: 'around 1845' without explanation of how this date was established from the cited source is opaque. Was it a specific year stated in the record, or derived from a census age? The report does not say. (3) Certainty language: 'definitely born' overclaims. No genealogical conclusion from a single source, particularly for Irish records in this period, warrants 'definitely'. 'The available evidence indicates' or 'is consistent with' would be appropriate. (4) Negative results: No mention of what other records were searched. Was civil registration (post-1864) checked? Were county Cork parish registers searched for multiple Murphy baptisms of the right period? Without this, the 'exhaustive search' requirement of GPS Step 1 cannot be assessed. (5) Alternative candidates: If there are multiple Bridget Murphy baptisms in county Cork c.1845 — which is likely, given how common both names are — the report must address whether the correct individual has been identified.

A professionally adequate report would: cite the specific record with full source details (church, parish, register series, date, folio or entry number, repository, access method and date); explain how the birth year was established; note other records searched and what they showed; acknowledge any alternative Bridget Murphy baptisms found and explain why the identified one is correct; and use appropriately qualified conclusion language.
learningObjectives: Describe the seven-section structure of a professional client research report.
Explain the role of negative results documentation in meeting GPS standards and serving future researchers.
Apply appropriate tone, register, and citation practice to genealogical report writing.
Evaluate a research report against professional standards, identifying specific deficiencies.
commonMistakes: Omitting negative results — the searches that found nothing are as important as those that found something.
Using vague source citations ('found on Ancestry', 'census records') instead of precise, locatable references.
Overclaiming certainty in conclusions — 'definitely' and 'proves' are rarely appropriate; 'the evidence indicates' and 'is consistent with' are more accurate.
Writing for a specialist audience when the client is a non-specialist — technical precision and accessibility are both required.
assessmentCriteria: Report structure includes all required sections with appropriate content in each.
All factual assertions are supported by citations in Evidence Explained format, sufficiently specific to locate the source.
Negative results are documented with sufficient detail to prevent duplication.
Conclusion language accurately reflects the evidential basis and avoids overclaiming.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: Standardised citation formats for genealogical sources, codified in Elizabeth Shown Mills's Evidence Explained (3rd ed., 2015) — the professional standard for source citation in genealogical reports.

A formal genealogical report for solicitors and probate courts identifying and proving the identity of heirs to an estate; held to legal evidentiary standards and may be scrutinised by opposing counsel.
A peer-reviewed analytical essay following GPS standards, as published in the National Genealogical Society Quarterly — the highest-prestige publication venue for genealogical research.

In client reports, endnotes keep citations from interrupting the narrative (preferred for non-specialist clients); in proof arguments and heir-location reports, footnotes keep citations close to the relevant assertion (preferred for specialist and legal readers).

questions.questionHtml: Why must a genealogical research report document searches that found nothing (negative results)?
options: To justify billing hours that produced no useful findings
Because GPS requires a reasonably exhaustive search — documenting negative results shows what was searched and prevents future researchers from duplicating work unnecessarily
Only heir-location reports require negative result documentation
Negative results are confidential and should not be shared with clients
questions.correctAnswer: Because GPS requires a reasonably exhaustive search — documenting negative results shows what was searched and prevents future researchers from duplicating work unnecessarily
questions.explanationHtml: A GPS-compliant report must demonstrate that the search was reasonably exhaustive. Documenting negative results — searches conducted that yielded nothing — both proves the completeness of the search and provides invaluable guidance for future researchers who would otherwise not know whether those sources had been checked.

questions.questionHtml: A research report concludes: 'I think Elizabeth was probably born in Yorkshire, but I'm not sure because I couldn't find her baptism anywhere.' What is wrong with this conclusion statement?
options: It is too short — conclusions must be at least one paragraph

It uses informal first-person language, fails to specify the evidential basis for the Yorkshire inference, and does not document what searches were conducted — all departures from professional report standards
The conclusion is acceptable for a client report even if it would not be acceptable for a proof argument
Professional reports should never express uncertainty
questions.correctAnswer: It uses informal first-person language, fails to specify the evidential basis for the Yorkshire inference, and does not document what searches were conducted — all departures from professional report standards
questions.explanationHtml: A professional report conclusion should: use third-person language; specify the evidence on which any inference is based; document what searches were conducted (particularly the negative ones); and use qualified but informative language ('the available evidence, while not conclusive, is consistent with a Yorkshire origin because...').

questions.questionHtml: Which citation is acceptable in a professional genealogical report?
options: 'Birth certificate for Thomas Hall, 1863, found on Ancestry.'

'England & Wales Birth Registration, Stoke-on-Trent district, December quarter 1863, vol. 6b, p. 157; General Register Office, Southport; digital image, Ancestry (www.ancestry.co.uk), accessed 3 May 2025.'
'GRO birth record, Stoke-on-Trent, 1863 — confirmed name and parents.'
'Family tree on Ancestry showing Thomas Hall born 1863, Stoke-on-Trent.'
questions.correctAnswer: 'England & Wales Birth Registration, Stoke-on-Trent district, December quarter 1863, vol. 6b, p. 157; General Register Office, Southport; digital image, Ancestry (www.ancestry.co.uk), accessed 3 May 2025.'
questions.explanationHtml: A professional citation must enable any researcher to locate the exact same record independently. It requires the record series, registration district, quarter/year, volume and page, repository, access method, and date accessed. Only the second option meets this standard.
